how-genai-interviews-have-shifted.explain:
## What it is

**What changed.** Early GenAI interviews tested whether you knew the vocabulary: transformers, attention, prompt tricks. Today most loops assume you can call a model and instead ask whether you can ship a system around one that stays correct, fast and affordable.

**What interviewers now probe**
- System design: a RAG or agent service with latency, cost and failure budgets.
- Evaluation: how you know a change helped, not just that a demo looks good.
- Debugging: given a symptom ("answers got worse last week"), how you isolate the stage.
- Judgement: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune, API vs self-hosted, workflow vs agent.

**Example.** Old question: "Explain self-attention." New question: "Your support bot hallucinates policy details for 3% of tickets. Walk me through finding out why."

**How it goes wrong.** Candidates over-index on model theory and cannot say how they would measure quality, or they recite a framework name without a trade-off. A good answer states the constraint, picks an option, names what it costs, and says how you would verify it.

reading-a-job-description.explain:
## What it is

**Why read it closely.** A job description (JD) is a compressed spec of the team's pain. The same title (AI Engineer, ML Engineer, GenAI Engineer) can mean building RAG backends, training models or doing analytics.

**How to decode one**
- **Verbs** tell you the work: "build, deploy, scale" means engineering; "experiment, model, analyse" leans data science.
- **Nouns** tell you the stack: vector DB, LangGraph, Kubernetes, vLLM, Airflow. Group them into must-have vs nice-to-have.
- **Scale hints**: "millions of users", "SLA", "on-call" signal production work; "POC", "stakeholders" signal early-stage.
- **Domain**: regulated industries (finance, health) imply privacy, audit and evaluation rigor.

**Example.** "Own the RAG platform, optimise latency and cost, partner with security" means expect design rounds on ingestion, caching, IAM, and cost questions.

**Failure modes.** Treating every bullet as mandatory, or preparing generically. Map each JD requirement to one project story of yours with a number (latency, accuracy, cost) so you can answer with evidence.

## What it is

**Three overlapping roles**
- **AI Engineer**: builds applications on top of foundation models: RAG, agents, tool use, evals, deployment, cost and latency. Strong software engineering, light on training.
- **GenAI Data Scientist**: experiments with prompts, fine-tuning, embedding choices and evaluation design; often owns offline metrics and prototypes, then hands over to engineering.
- **Data Scientist (classical)**: statistics, forecasting, classification, experimentation (A/B tests), feature engineering; LLMs are one tool among many.

**Where they overlap.** All three should reason about evaluation and data quality. They differ in what they are accountable for: the AI engineer for the running service, the GenAI DS for the model/prompt quality evidence, the DS for the analytical insight.

**Why it matters in an interview.** Titles vary by company, so ask what the team ships. If you are a software engineer with 4+ years, the AI Engineer path usually fits best: you reuse your backend, API and reliability skills.

**Failure mode.** Pitching yourself as all three. Pick the lane the JD describes and show adjacent depth.

why-the-engineering-layer-dominates.explain:
## What it is

**Claim.** In most production GenAI systems, the model is a commodity call and the surrounding engineering decides whether the product works.

**Why**
- Frontier and open models are accessible by API; differences between providers are often smaller than differences in your retrieval quality, prompts and data.
- Failures are usually system failures: stale index, bad chunking, timeouts, retries that multiply cost, missing permissions, no fallback.
- Quality is sustained by evals, monitoring, caching, rate limiting and rollbacks, none of which the model gives you.

**Example (illustrative).** A team swaps to a bigger model and gains a little; fixing chunking and adding a reranker gains far more at lower cost.

**Interview use.** When asked about improving a system, start from the pipeline and measurements, not the model. 

**Caveat.** This does not mean models never matter: for narrow tasks, latency-critical paths or privacy limits, model choice and adaptation are central. The point is the order of investigation: data and system first.

api-hosted-vs-self-hosted-models.explain:
## What it is

**Two ways to get inference.** *API-hosted*: a provider runs the model; you pay per token. *Self-hosted*: you run an open-weight model on your own GPUs (vLLM, TGI, cloud endpoints).

**API-hosted strengths**: fastest start, best frontier quality, no GPU ops, elastic scale. **Weaknesses**: per-token cost at volume, data leaves your boundary, rate limits, vendor changes or deprecations, limited customisation.

**Self-hosted strengths**: data control, predictable cost at steady high volume, fine-tuning freedom, no external rate limits. **Weaknesses**: GPU capacity planning, utilisation, batching, upgrades, on-call, and typically a quality gap on hard tasks.

**Deciding**
- Low or spiky volume, need best quality: API.
- Strict data residency, high steady throughput, narrow task: self-host (or a private endpoint from a cloud provider).
- Often hybrid: self-hosted small model for routine traffic, API model for hard cases.

**Interview angle.** Do a rough cost break-even with labelled assumptions (tokens per day, GPU hourly price, utilisation), and mention ops burden. Self-hosting at 10% GPU utilisation is usually more expensive than the API.

## What it is

**Problem.** Enterprise content is PDFs with tables, scanned images, slide decks, wikis, tickets and spreadsheets, each with different permissions and update rates. RAG quality is capped by how well this is turned into clean, attributable chunks.

**Pipeline**
1. **Connectors** pull from sources incrementally (change feeds or modified-time cursors) instead of full re-crawls.
2. **Parsing**: layout-aware extraction for PDFs and tables, OCR for scans; keep structure (headings, table rows) as metadata.
3. **Cleaning and dedup**: strip boilerplate headers/footers, hash near-duplicate documents.
4. **Chunking** by structure (section, table) with overlap only where it helps.
5. **Metadata**: source, version, owner, ACL, timestamp, so you can filter and cite.
6. **Embed and index**, with a content hash to skip unchanged chunks.

**Why it matters.** Wrong table parsing or lost ACLs produce confident wrong answers or data leaks.

**Failure modes.** Re-embedding everything nightly (cost), stale deletions (removed docs still retrievable), OCR noise, and ACLs not carried to chunks. Use a dead-letter queue for documents that fail parsing and track ingestion success rate.

**Question shape.** "Your RAG system must serve 5,000 concurrent users." Answer by finding the bottleneck at each hop.

**Where load lands**
- **LLM calls**: the slowest and costliest. Provider rate limits (requests and tokens per minute) cap throughput; self-hosted needs GPU batching.

- **Embedding the query**: small but on the critical path; batch and cache.

**Concurrent is not requests/sec.** Convert: concurrency is about rate times latency (Little's law). 5,000 users who each ask once per minute is far less than 5,000 simultaneous calls.

**A reasonable decomposition**

## What it is

**Principle.** Keep request-handling services **stateless** and push state into dedicated stores. Then any replica can serve any request and you can autoscale, restart and deploy freely.

**State that exists in a RAG/agent system**
- Documents and files: object storage.
- Embeddings: vector store.
- Metadata, users, conversations: a database.
- Hot data (sessions, cache, rate-limit counters): in-memory store such as Redis.
- Job state: queue plus a status table.

**Why it matters.** If conversation history lives in an API pod's memory, a restart loses it and sticky sessions are needed, which hurts scaling.

**How.** Pass a conversation ID; the service loads history from the store, runs the step, and writes back. Make writes idempotent so retries are safe.

**Failure modes.** Hidden local state (in-process caches that diverge, local files), unbounded history growth, and a stateful store becoming the single point of failure without replication or backups.

asynchronous-messaging-queues.explain:
## What it is

**Why queues.** Some work is slow or bursty: document ingestion, embedding batches, report generation, long agent runs. A queue decouples the producer from consumers so spikes are absorbed and workers scale independently.

**Core ideas**
- **Producer** enqueues a job and returns a job ID; **workers** consume; the client polls or receives a callback/stream.
- **At-least-once delivery** means duplicates happen, so handlers must be **idempotent**.
- **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter**, with a max attempts count.
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)** collects poison messages for inspection.
- **Backpressure**: bounded queues and rate limits protect downstream LLM quotas.
- **Visibility timeout**: a job not acknowledged in time returns to the queue.

**Example.** Upload 10,000 PDFs: enqueue one message per document; workers parse and embed; progress is tracked in a status table.

**Failure modes.** Unbounded queue growth hiding an outage, retry storms against a rate-limited provider, and non-idempotent writes creating duplicate chunks. Alert on queue depth and age of oldest message.

## What it is

**Idea.** Every dependency fails sometimes. A fallback is a pre-planned degraded behaviour that keeps the user served.

**Fallback ladder for a RAG answer**
1. Primary LLM times out: retry once quickly with a budget.
2. Switch to a **secondary provider or smaller model**.
3. Serve a **cached answer** for a similar question.
4. Return **retrieved passages only** (search results) without generation.
5. Show an honest error with a retry option.

**Supporting patterns**
- **Timeouts** on every call, with a total request deadline.
- **Circuit breaker**: after repeated failures stop calling for a cool-off period.
- **Health checks and routing** at the LLM gateway.
- **Feature flags** to switch behaviour without deploy.

**Trade-offs.** Fallback models may differ in quality, format or safety behaviour, so evaluate them in advance and normalise output schema. Fallbacks can also raise cost.

**Failure modes.** Retrying forever, cascading failure when all callers retry at once, and untested fallback paths that break when first used. Test them with fault injection.

## What it is

**Pick the store for the access pattern.**
- **Object storage** (S3-like): raw files, parsed text, snapshots. Cheap, durable, not queryable.
- **Vector store**: nearest-neighbour search on embeddings (HNSW/IVF indexes). Good for semantic similarity; supports metadata filters.
- **Keyword/search engine** (BM25, inverted index): exact terms, IDs, codes, rare words where embeddings struggle.
- **Graph database**: entities and relationships for multi-hop questions ("which contracts involve vendors owned by X"), used in graph-RAG.
- **Relational DB**: users, permissions, jobs, conversation metadata, transactions.

**Hybrid retrieval.** Combine keyword and vector results (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) then rerank; this typically beats either alone on enterprise data.

**Trade-offs.** One database that does everything (e.g. Postgres with pgvector) reduces operations at small scale; dedicated vector DBs help at large scale or special filtering needs. Every extra store adds sync complexity.

**Failure modes.** Index and source of truth drifting apart, embedding model changes requiring full re-index (version your embeddings), and using vectors for exact-match lookup.

## What it is

networking-iam.explain:
## What it is

**Goal.** Only the right callers reach the right resources, with the least privilege.

**Networking**
- Put data stores and workers in **private subnets**; expose only the gateway.
- Use **private endpoints/VPC connectivity** to cloud model APIs where available so traffic avoids the public internet.
- Egress control: allow-list outbound domains (important for agents and tools to limit exfiltration and SSRF).
- TLS everywhere, including internal hops when required.

**IAM**
- Each service has its own **role**; grant only needed actions on specific resources.
- Prefer short-lived credentials from a workload identity over long-lived keys.
- **User-level authorisation in retrieval**: filter chunks by the user's permissions so the LLM never sees documents the user cannot access.
- Separate environments and accounts for dev, staging, prod.

**Failure modes.** Over-broad roles ("*" permissions), a shared service key, retrieval that ignores ACLs (the model leaks restricted content), and open egress letting a prompt-injected agent call arbitrary hosts.

## What it is

**Secrets** are API keys for LLM providers, database passwords and signing keys. They must never be in code, images, logs or prompts.

**Practices**
- Store in a **secrets manager** (cloud KMS-backed, Vault); inject at runtime via environment or mounted file.
- **Rotate** regularly and on suspected leak; support two active keys during rotation.
- Scope keys per service and environment; set provider spend limits.
- Scan repos and CI for leaked secrets; redact secrets in logs.

**Encryption**
- **In transit**: TLS.
- **At rest**: encrypted object storage, databases and vector stores; managed keys, or customer-managed keys for regulated data.
- Consider field-level encryption or tokenisation for highly sensitive fields, and remember embeddings can leak information about source text, so treat the vector store as sensitive.

**Failure modes.** A key committed to git (rotate immediately, history remains), one shared key for all environments, logs capturing full prompts with PII, and no key budget limit leading to a cost explosion if a key leaks.

**CI/CD for LLM systems** covers code, prompts, models and indexes.

- Immutable images, **infrastructure as code**, environment promotion dev, staging, prod.
- **Progressive rollout**: canary or percentage rollout, shadow traffic for a new model or prompt, with automatic rollback on SLO burn.
- **Versioning** of prompts, model IDs, embedding models and index builds so a rollback restores a consistent set.
- Feature flags for model/prompt switches.

**Failure modes.** Prompts edited in a dashboard without review, evals nondeterministic enough to flap (use fixed seeds, thresholds, repeated runs), and deploying a new embedding model without re-indexing. Treat prompt changes like code changes.

## What it is

**Scenario.** "The RAG assistant was good at launch; a week later users say quality fell." Nothing was deployed. This is a classic **drift** question.

**Candidate causes**
- **Data drift**: new or changed documents ingested badly (parse failures, duplicates, stale or missing updates, deletions not applied).
- **Query drift**: users ask different things than the eval set covered.
- **Upstream model change**: provider silently updated a model alias.
- **Infrastructure**: index degraded, timeouts producing truncated context, cache serving stale answers, a rate-limit fallback to a weaker model.
- **Feedback loop** or prompt/config change by someone.

1. Define the symptom with data: which metric, which queries, since when.
2. Build a timeline of changes (deploys, ingestion, model versions, traffic mix).
3. Replay a fixed eval set today versus launch to separate system change from query change.

## What it is

**Method.** A RAG answer passes through stages: query understanding, retrieval, reranking, context assembly, generation, post-processing. Evaluate each separately so you fix the right one.

**Checks per stage**
- **Retrieval**: is the gold passage in the top-k? (recall@k, hit rate). If not, the generator cannot succeed: look at chunking, embedding, filters, hybrid search.
- **Reranking**: is the gold passage in the context after reranking and is it ranked high?
- **Context assembly**: truncation, ordering, duplicates, prompt injection in documents.
- **Generation**: given the gold context, does the model answer faithfully? If not, prompt or model issue.

**Technique.** Take failing examples and label where the first fault occurs; tally by stage. This points to the largest fixable share. Use component-level metrics (recall@k, context precision, faithfulness) and traces.

**Failure modes.** Tuning prompts for what is actually a retrieval miss, and judging only end-to-end scores which cannot say where to act.

designing-an-agent-for-a-business-task.explain:
## What it is

**Approach.** Start from the task, not the framework. Example prompt: "Design an agent that handles refund requests."

**Steps**
1. **Define the job and success**: inputs, allowed outcomes, metrics (resolution rate, accuracy, cost, escalation rate).
2. **Map the process** a human follows; identify decision points and the systems touched.
3. **Choose tools** narrowly: lookup_order, check_policy, issue_refund (with limits). Give each a clear schema and description.
4. **Control flow**: fixed steps where the process is known, model decisions only where judgement is needed.
5. **Guardrails**: input validation, permission scopes, amount caps, human approval for risky actions.
6. **Evaluation**: a test set of real cases, scoring final outcome and trajectory; replay before shipping.
7. **Operations**: logging, cost budget, step limits, escalation path.

**Interview tip.** State what the agent must never do and where a human signs off. Mention starting with a read-only or assist mode, then widening autonomy as eval evidence accumulates.

**Failure modes.** Giving a broad tool set up front, no success metric, and shipping without trajectory logs.

Agent interviews: design for a business task, defend workflow vs autonomous, tools/MCP/memory/multi-agent, then the failure list — loops, bad tool choice, tool errors, nondeterministic trajectories, cost, context rot, over-powered tools. HITL on consequential actions. Debug from a trajectory. Know when not to go autonomous. Traps: citing a title you never retrieved; calling a workflow an agent.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Designing an agent for a business task. Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, designing an agent for a business task is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. The tell is whether you reach for a graph of agents before a flowchart.

The concrete requirement is: Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, workflow or agent, and the trap of mixing the words. A strong answer names this item (Designing an agent for a business task) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Designing an agent for a business task” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution.

Write the task. If the graph is stable, draw a workflow. If it is not, add an agent with caps and HITL. Walk one trajectory that failed in prod.

Refunds under $20 are a workflow. Refunds over $200 with a write tool are HITL. You do not add a researcher agent to look stylish.

Write the control in the release notes for m15-3: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “Designing an agent for a business task” because the happy path works.** Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution. Calling a four-step DAG an agent.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. No spend cap in the design.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement designing an agent for a business task. Citing a doc title that was never in the retrieved set.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Designing an agent for a business task: Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution. workflow-or-autonomous-agent.explain:
## What it is

**Distinction.** A **workflow** orchestrates LLM calls and tools along predefined code paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallel steps). An **agent** lets the model decide the next step and tool in a loop until it judges the task done.

**Choose a workflow when** the steps are known, predictability, cost and testability matter, or the domain is regulated. It is cheaper, faster and easier to debug.

**Choose an agent when** the path cannot be predicted in advance (open-ended research, debugging code), the task has many branches, and you can tolerate variance and higher cost.

**Spectrum.** Many good systems are workflows with a small agentic step inside (e.g. a fixed pipeline where only the "investigate" step loops with a step limit).

**Rule of thumb.** Use the simplest thing that works: single call, then workflow, then agent only if evaluation shows workflows cannot reach the target.

**Failure modes.** Using an agent for a deterministic process (cost and flakiness for nothing), or a rigid workflow for open-ended tasks that leaves many cases unhandled.

tools-mcp-memory-multi-agent.explain:
## What it is

**Four building blocks**
- **Tools**: functions the model can call, defined by name, description and JSON schema. Quality of descriptions largely determines selection accuracy. Return concise, structured results.
- **MCP (Model Context Protocol)**: an open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts from servers to AI clients in a standard way, so integrations are reusable across applications. Treat third-party servers as untrusted, and scope permissions.
- **Memory**: short-term (the context window/conversation state) and long-term (stored facts or summaries retrieved when relevant). Needs write policies, expiry and privacy controls.
- **Multi-agent**: several agents with distinct roles (planner, worker, reviewer) or an orchestrator delegating to sub-agents with focused contexts.

**When multi-agent helps**: parallelisable subtasks, separate contexts to avoid overload, specialised tools. **Cost**: more tokens, coordination bugs, harder debugging.

**Interview tip.** Default to a single agent with good tools; justify multi-agent by a concrete bottleneck.

**Failure modes.** Too many overlapping tools, unbounded memory that pollutes context, agents passing lossy summaries to each other.

|---|---|---|

runaway-loops.explain:
## What it is

**What it is.** The agent keeps calling tools or retrying the same plan without making progress, burning tokens and time.

**Causes**
- No clear termination criteria or the model cannot recognise done.
- A tool returns an unhelpful error or empty result and the agent retries identically.
- Conflicting instructions, or a goal that is impossible.
- Context growth pushes the original goal out of focus.

**Defences**
- **Hard limits**: max steps, max tokens/cost, wall-clock timeout.
- **Loop detection**: same tool and arguments repeated N times, or no new information in M steps; then change strategy or escalate.
- **Helpful tool errors** that say what to do differently ("no results for X; try broader query").
- Explicit **stop conditions** and a final-answer tool.
- Escalate to a human with the trajectory so far.

**Example.** An agent searches "invoice 123" three times with identical empty results. A loop detector triggers: it should either broaden the query or report not found.

**Failure mode.** Relying only on max-steps, which prevents infinite cost but still wastes the budget and returns nothing useful.

poor-tool-selection.explain:
## What it is

**Symptom.** The agent calls the wrong tool, skips a needed one, or passes bad arguments.

**Causes**
- **Too many tools** (dozens) or overlapping ones with similar descriptions.
- Descriptions that explain what the tool is called, not when to use it and when not to.
- Ambiguous parameter names, missing types, enums or examples.
- Tool outputs that are huge or unclear, misleading the next step.

**Fixes**
- Reduce and consolidate tools; give each a distinct purpose.
- Write descriptions as guidance: when to use, inputs with examples, what it returns, limits.
- Use strict schemas with enums and validation, returning clear errors for bad arguments.
- **Retrieve tools dynamically** or route to sub-agents when the toolset is big.
- Build an eval of tool-selection cases (expected tool and args) and track accuracy.

**Interview tip.** Treat tool design like API design for a user who reads only the docs. A model-level fix (bigger model) is a last resort after tool and prompt fixes.

tool-failures.explain:
## What it is

**Reality.** Tools time out, return 5xx, rate limit, return malformed data or partial results. An agent that assumes success will hallucinate around the gap.

**Handling**
- **Classify errors**: transient (timeout, 429, 503) versus permanent (bad arguments, not found, unauthorised).
- **Transient**: retry with backoff and jitter inside the tool wrapper, with a cap.
- **Permanent**: return a structured, informative error to the model; do not retry blindly.
- **Timeouts** on every tool call; circuit breakers for repeatedly failing dependencies.
- **Idempotency keys** for side-effecting tools so a retry cannot double-charge or double-send.
- **Validate outputs** against a schema before giving them to the model.
- **Graceful degradation**: alternate tool or tell the user what could not be done.

**Example.** A payment tool times out. Without idempotency the agent retries and refunds twice; with an idempotency key the second call is a no-op.

**Failure modes.** Swallowing errors so the model invents an answer, and leaking stack traces or secrets to the model in error text.

nondeterministic-trajectories.explain:
## What it is

**What it is.** The same input can produce different sequences of thoughts, tool calls and answers across runs because of sampling and branching decisions. A small early difference compounds.

**Implications**
- A single successful run proves little; measure **pass rate over multiple trials** (and consistency, e.g. pass^k meaning all k runs succeed, for reliability-critical use).
- Regression tests flake if they assert exact trajectories.

**Controls**
- Lower temperature; fixed seeds where supported (not guaranteed).
- Constrain with **structured outputs** and deterministic workflow steps.
- Evaluate **outcomes** (state of the system, correct final answer) rather than exact step sequences, plus sanity checks on the trajectory (no forbidden tools, within budget).
- Record full traces to replay and diff.
- Keep temperature 0 for tool-calling steps where creativity is not needed.

**Interview tip.** Say that you accept variance in the path but not in safety-critical outcomes, so you add validation and approval gates at those points.

**Failure modes.** Declaring success from one demo, or asserting exact tool order in tests.

excessive-token-cost-usage.explain:
## What it is

**Why agents are expensive.** Each loop iteration resends the growing context (system prompt, tool schemas, history, tool outputs), so cost grows roughly quadratically with steps if nothing is trimmed.

**Cost drivers**
- Long tool outputs (full web pages, large JSON) pasted into context.
- Many steps from loops or poor planning.
- Large tool schemas on every call.
- Using the biggest model for every step.

**Reductions**
- **Trim and summarise** tool outputs; return only needed fields.
- **Prompt caching** for the stable prefix (system prompt, tools) where the provider supports it; check current docs.
- **Route models**: small model for routine steps, large for hard reasoning.
- **Step and budget limits**; cheaper retrieval before expensive reasoning.
- Compact history by summarising older turns.
- Track **cost per task** and p95 outliers, alert on spikes.

**Example (illustrative).** 20 steps each re-sending 10k tokens is 200k input tokens for one task; trimming outputs to 2k cuts that to ~40k.

**Failure mode.** Optimising average cost while a few runaway tasks create the bulk of spend.

context-degradation.explain:
## What it is

**What it is.** As the context fills with history and tool outputs, model performance on later steps often drops: it loses the original goal, ignores instructions buried in the middle, or gets distracted by irrelevant text.

**Symptoms.** Forgetting constraints given early, repeating work, contradicting earlier decisions, drifting off task in long sessions.

**Mitigations**
- **Keep context lean**: concise tool outputs, remove stale content.
- **Summarise or checkpoint** progress and decisions periodically, then continue from the summary (watch for lossy summaries).
- Place critical instructions where they are noticed (start and restated near the end), and restate the goal and plan.
- **External memory**: store notes or a task list outside the window and retrieve what is needed.
- **Sub-agents** with fresh, focused contexts for isolated subtasks, returning short results.
- Retrieve rather than stuff documents.

**Interview tip.** Bigger context windows do not remove this; measure with long-horizon evals.

**Failure modes.** Summaries that drop a crucial constraint, and memory stores that retrieve irrelevant or outdated facts.

overly-powerful-tool-permissions.explain:
## What it is

**Risk.** An agent with a general `run_sql`, `shell` or `send_email` tool can do anything its credentials allow. Prompt injection from a web page or document, or a plain mistake, then becomes data loss or exfiltration.

**Principles**
- **Least privilege**: narrow tools (`get_order_status`, not arbitrary SQL), read-only by default, scoped credentials per tool and per user.
- **Limits** in code: amount caps, rate limits, allow-listed recipients/domains, row limits.
- **Authorisation on behalf of the user**: the tool checks the end user's rights, not the agent's.
- **Approval gates** for destructive or irreversible actions.
- **Sandboxing** for code execution (no network, limited filesystem, time limits).
- **Treat tool outputs and retrieved text as untrusted** and separate them from instructions.
- Audit logs for every action.

**Interview tip.** Security cannot rely on the prompt saying "do not delete". Enforce in the tool layer.

**Failure modes.** A shared admin credential, tools that accept free-form commands, and agents that can both read untrusted content and send data out (the "lethal trifecta" style exposure with private data).

human-in-the-loop-checkpoints.explain:
## What it is

**Idea.** Insert human review at points where error cost is high, so autonomy applies where it is safe.

**Where to place checkpoints**
- Irreversible or high-impact actions: payments above a threshold, deleting data, external communication, production changes.
- Low-confidence or ambiguous situations the agent detects.
- Policy-sensitive decisions (legal, medical, compliance).
- Plan approval before a long expensive run.

**Design**
- The agent **pauses and persists state**, presents a clear summary (proposed action, evidence, alternatives) and waits for approve, edit or reject.

## What it is

**Trajectory** = the full record of a run: user input, model messages, tool calls with arguments, tool results, token counts, timings, errors. It is the debugger for agents.

**Procedure**
1. Pull the trace of a failing run (tracing tools or your own logs).
2. Walk step by step and find the **first step** where behaviour became wrong, since later steps usually just follow.

**Interview tip.** Describe aggregating many trajectories to spot patterns, e.g. 40% of failures begin with the same wrong tool.

## What it is

**Core point.** Autonomy is a cost, not a goal. Do not use an autonomous agent when a simpler or safer design meets the need.

**Avoid full autonomy when**
- The process is deterministic and well understood: write a workflow or plain code.
- Errors are costly or irreversible and you cannot verify outputs cheaply.
- Strict latency or cost budgets leave no room for loops.
- Regulation demands auditability and deterministic behaviour.
- You lack an evaluation set; you cannot tell whether it works.
- Tools are too powerful to scope safely.

**Alternatives**
- Single LLM call with structured output.
- Fixed workflow (chaining/routing).
- Assistant that proposes, human decides.
- Agent confined to read-only research with a final human step.

prompt-vs-rag-vs-fine-tuning.explain:
## What it is

**Three levers, different problems.**
- **Prompting** (instructions, examples, structure): fixes *how the model behaves* on the task. Cheapest, fastest to iterate.
- **RAG**: gives the model *knowledge it lacks* (private, fresh, large corpora) at query time, with citations and easy updates.
- **Fine-tuning**: changes *model behaviour or style persistently*: output format, tone, domain skill, latency/cost via a smaller model.

**Decision order.** Try prompting first with an eval set. If errors are due to missing facts, add RAG. If the model still cannot follow the format/style/skill consistently, or you need a smaller faster model, consider fine-tuning. They combine: a fine-tuned model with RAG.

**Common misconception.** Fine-tuning is not a good way to add facts: it is lossy, hard to update and cannot cite. Use RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour.

**Interview tip.** Ask: is the failure about knowledge, behaviour or cost? Then justify the lever and how you would measure improvement.

**Failure modes.** Fine-tuning before building evals, and using RAG for a pure style problem.

Prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune from a brief. Tune when behaviour is stable and cheaper rungs failed. LoRA/QLoRA/PEFT/quant as engineering trade-offs. Deploying a tuned open-weight model is serving, GPUs, latency, cost. “Accuracy dropped after deploy” is data, format, shift, eval, inference config, serving, quant. Refuse to tune when labels are thin or RAG already owns freshness. LoRA in 60 seconds: low-rank adapters, what you freeze, how you eval forgetting.

lora-qlora-peft-quantization.explain:
## What it is

**PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning)** trains a small number of added parameters while freezing the base model, cutting memory and cost.

**LoRA**: adds low-rank matrices to selected weight matrices (e.g. attention projections). Instead of updating a d-by-d matrix, learn two small matrices of rank r, so trainable parameters are a tiny fraction. Adapters can be swapped or merged into the base weights.

**QLoRA**: keep the frozen base model **quantized** (e.g. 4-bit) and train LoRA adapters in higher precision, allowing fine-tuning of large models on a single GPU with modest quality loss.

**Quantization** reduces numeric precision of weights (16-bit to 8 or 4-bit) to cut memory and often speed up inference, with some accuracy loss that must be measured. It applies to serving too, not just training.

**Key knobs**: rank r, alpha, target modules, learning rate, epochs. Higher rank gives more capacity and cost.

**Trade-offs.** Full fine-tuning can reach higher quality but needs much more memory and storage per variant; LoRA stores small adapters per task.

**Failure modes.** Overfitting on small data, forgetting general ability, evaluating only on training-like data, and not testing the quantized model that you will actually serve.

deploying-a-fine-tuned-open-weight-model.explain:
## What it is

**From adapter to production.**

**Serving stack.** An inference server such as vLLM or TGI (check current options) that supports continuous batching and efficient KV-cache use. Load the base model plus LoRA adapters, or merge adapters, and optionally serve several adapters on one base.

**Steps**
1. **Package**: model weights, tokenizer, chat template (a template mismatch is a classic silent bug), config, pinned library versions.
2. **Size hardware**: weights memory plus KV cache for expected concurrency and context length; choose quantization to fit.
3. **Benchmark** latency (time to first token, tokens per second) and throughput under realistic load.
4. **Release safely**: shadow or canary against the current model, compare metrics, keep rollback.
5. **Operate**: autoscale on queue depth or GPU utilisation, health checks, GPU monitoring, model registry with versions.
6. **Safety**: guardrails and moderation are yours to add; open weights do not include a provider's filters.

**Failure modes.** Different prompt format than training, merged-adapter quantization degrading quality, cold-start load times for large weights, and GPUs idle at low traffic.

accuracy-dropped-after-deployment.explain:
## What it is

**Scenario.** "Offline accuracy was 92%; a week after deployment live accuracy looks like 80%." Think of three buckets: *the model is the same but inputs changed*, *the serving differs from training/eval*, *measurement is different*.

**Causes**
- **Distribution shift**: live queries differ from training and eval data (new topics, languages, formats).
- **Training-serving skew**: different preprocessing, prompt template, tokenizer, quantization, truncation or context length.
- **Eval leakage** that made offline numbers too optimistic.
- **Metric mismatch**: how live correctness is labelled (user feedback, sampled review) differs from offline labels.
- **Upstream changes**: retrieval index, tools, data formats.
- **Infrastructure**: timeouts, fallbacks to another model, batch or precision bugs.

**First moves.** Replay the offline set against the live stack; if it still scores 92%, the model is fine and the data shifted; if lower, suspect skew or infra. Segment errors by input type, time and version.

**Prevention.** Monitor input distributions, keep a live-sampled labelled set, and run canary comparisons.

## What it is

**A checklist for post-deployment accuracy drops** (or any fine-tuned model regression).

1. **What changed?** Model version, adapter, quantization, prompt template, retrieval index, tools, traffic source, upstream data.
2. **Is the metric real?** Check label source, sample size and confidence intervals; weekly noise can look like a drop.
3. **Input distribution**: compare live inputs to training/eval (length, language, topic, format) using embeddings or simple statistics.
4. **Segments**: accuracy by customer, intent, language, input length; find where the drop concentrates.
5. **Serving parity**: run the same examples via offline and online paths and diff outputs.
6. **Error taxonomy**: sample 50 failures, label causes (format, knowledge, reasoning, truncated context).
7. **Dependencies**: provider or tool outages, fallback model usage rates.
8. **Decide**: roll back if user harm is significant; otherwise patch (prompt, filter, data) and retrain with new live examples.

**Interview tip.** Present as a hypothesis tree ordered by cheapness to test, and say what evidence would confirm each.

**Failure mode.** Retraining immediately without knowing the cause, which may bake in the bug.

## What it is

**Incident method.** Stabilise first, understand second.

1. **Detect and declare**: alert or report; assign an incident lead; open a channel and timeline.
2. **Scope impact**: who is affected, which endpoints/models/regions, since when, severity.
3. **Mitigate quickly**: rollback the last change, flip a feature flag, shift traffic to a fallback, rate limit, scale up. Do not wait for root cause when users are hurt.
4. **Diagnose**: compare against the change log (deploys, config, prompts, model aliases, ingestion, traffic spikes), read traces and metrics by stage (gateway, retrieval, LLM, GPU), check dependencies' status pages.
5. **Resolve and verify** with the same signals that raised the alert.
6. **Postmortem** (blameless): timeline, root cause, contributing factors, detection gap, action items with owners.

**LLM-specific causes**: provider outage or rate limit, model alias updated, prompt change, token explosion from a long document, cache or vector index issue, GPU memory pressure.

**Interview tip.** Say mitigate then investigate, and describe how you would prevent recurrence (alerts, canaries, limits).

**Failure mode.** Debugging live while users still suffer, or changing several things at once and losing causality.

**Three classic production symptoms and first suspects.**

**Latency spikes**
- Provider slowdowns or queueing; large prompts (context growth, retrieval returning too much); retries stacking; cold starts; GPU saturation or long generations; noisy neighbours.
- Check p95/p99 by stage, input and output token counts, queue depth, time to first token.

**Outages**
- Provider outage or auth/quota exhaustion (expired key, spend cap); DNS or network config; deploy bug; dependency (vector DB) down; crash loops from memory.
- Check error rates by code (429, 5xx, timeouts), health checks, recent changes.

**Cost explosions**
- Runaway agent loops, retry storms, missing caching, prompt bloat, switch to a pricier model, abuse or a leaked key, background job reprocessing everything.
- Check tokens and cost by tenant/feature/model, top spenders, request volume anomalies.

fallbacks-retries-autoscaling.explain:
## What it is

**Three resilience tools and their interactions.**

**Retries**: for transient errors only (timeouts, 429, 503). Use exponential backoff with jitter, a small max attempts, and a per-request deadline. Honour `Retry-After`. Ensure idempotency. Retries amplify load, so budget them (retry budget as a fraction of traffic).

**Fallbacks**: alternate model or provider, cache, or reduced functionality (see degrade ladder). Route via a gateway with health-based failover and circuit breakers.

**Autoscaling**: scale stateless services on CPU, requests or queue depth. For self-hosted LLMs scale on GPU utilisation or queue length/pending requests; GPU nodes start slowly (minutes for model load), so keep warm capacity and scale early. Set max replicas to protect budgets.

**Interactions to reason about**
- Retries plus autoscaling can mask a problem or cause a thundering herd.
- Fallback to a weaker model needs quality alerts.
- Scaling cannot beat an external provider's rate limit.

**Failure modes.** Retrying non-idempotent calls, no jitter, scale-to-zero on latency-critical paths, and untested failover.

reading-monitoring-signals.explain:
## What it is

**Signals worth knowing**
- **Traffic**: requests per second, tokens per request, by tenant/feature.
- **Latency**: p50/p95/p99, time to first token, tokens per second; per stage.
- **Errors**: rate by code (4xx vs 5xx, 429), timeouts, guardrail blocks.
- **Saturation**: queue depth, GPU utilisation and memory, KV-cache usage, concurrency.
- **Cost**: dollars per request, per tenant, per model.
- **Quality**: online eval scores, thumbs up/down, citation/groundedness rates, escalation rate, fallback rate.

**Reading them together**
- Latency up and tokens per request up: prompt/context growth.
- Latency up and GPU queue up: capacity.
- 429s rising: you are hitting provider limits.
- Traffic flat, cost up: model change, loops or longer outputs.
- Errors flat but thumbs-down up: a quality problem, not an availability problem.

**Pitfalls.** Averages hide tails; dashboards without version annotations hide causes; too many alerts cause fatigue. Annotate deploys and prompt/model changes on graphs.

alert-rollback-or-investigate.explain:
## What it is

**Decision framework** when an alert fires.

1. **Is it real and user-facing?** Confirm with a second signal or a synthetic probe.
2. **Severity**: size of impact and rate of worsening; SLO burn rate.
3. **Was there a recent change?** If strongly correlated and the change is reversible, **roll back** (or flip the flag) first; it is the fastest safe mitigation.
4. **No change or rollback not helping**: **investigate** with traces and dependency checks while applying generic mitigations (scale, shed load, fallback).
5. **Minor or noisy**: acknowledge, ticket, tune the alert.

**Alert quality.** Page on symptoms tied to SLOs (error budget burn), not causes; each alert needs a runbook and an owner. Multi-window burn-rate alerts reduce noise.

**LLM nuance.** Prompt and model changes are deployable artifacts, so keep them rollbackable. Provider-side changes you cannot roll back, so use fallbacks and pinned versions.

**Failure modes.** Rolling back a change unrelated to the issue, ignoring slow burns, and alert fatigue.

proprietary-api-vs-self-hosted-inference.explain:
## What it is

**Operational comparison in production.**

**Proprietary API**
- Pros: no GPU management, elastic capacity, strong models, quick updates.
- Cons: rate limits and provider outages beyond your control, model deprecations and silent behaviour changes, per-token cost, data governance review, limited latency control.
- Operational answer: gateway with multi-provider failover, pinned model versions, budgets, caching, regional endpoints, contract and data-processing terms.

**Self-hosted**
- Pros: control over latency, versions and data; stable behaviour; fixed-cost capacity at high utilisation.
- Cons: capacity planning, GPU scarcity and cost, slow scale-up, kernel/driver/runtime upgrades, on-call, and building safety and evals yourself.
- Operational answer: inference server with continuous batching, quantization, autoscaling on queue, warm replicas, model registry, canary rollouts.

**Break-even thinking (illustrative).** Compare monthly API token spend to GPU hours at realistic utilisation plus engineering time. Include peak capacity, not only average.

**Hybrid.** Self-host a tuned small model for the bulk; route hard queries to an API model; use each as the other's failover.

**Interview tip.** State assumptions and what would flip the decision.

## What it is

Debug a quality drop in this order: **pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix**. Starting at “the model got worse” is the junior path.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, interview is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. They want a first five minutes, not a memoir.

The concrete requirement is: Debug a quality drop in this order: **pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix**. Starting at “the model got worse” is the junior path. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, debug a quality drop in that order, then an incident story with a case you added. A strong answer names this item (interview) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Memorise the order. Example: pin flat, index new → rebuild index; do not tune.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “interview” because the happy path works.** Debug a quality drop in this order: **pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix**. Starting at “the model got worse” is the junior path. Starting at the model weights.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. A story with no pin or no case added.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement interview. Retry storms without jitter or a cap.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Quality drop: pin, retrieval, prompt id, traffic mix.

## A concrete walk-through

You recite the four and stop. They will go deeper; you already look organised.

They push back: “Do we really need interview?” They ask about self-host. You compare privacy and tail latency, and you do not pretend it deletes LLMOps. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Debug a quality drop in this order: **pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix**. Starting at “the model got worse” is the junior path. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

Whether your first four checks are in the right order, and whether the story includes a new gold case. Also: time since you last exercised “interview” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “interview” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

Memorise the order until it is muscle memory: pin, retrieval, prompt id, traffic mix. Starting at “the model got worse” is the junior path. Recite the four and then take their deeper question.

## What it is

**What it is:** System-design prompts are deliberately vague ("design a support assistant"). Your first job is to convert vagueness into explicit, checkable assumptions.

**How it works:** Spend 3-5 minutes asking about the axes that change the architecture:
- **Users and scale:** who, how many, requests per second (illustrative: 50 RPS peak vs 5,000).
- **Data:** what sources, how fresh, how sensitive, how large.
- **Quality bar:** is a wrong answer annoying or costly (legal, medical)?
- **Latency and cost budgets:** chat needs a first token under ~2 s; batch can take hours.
- **Constraints:** region, compliance, existing stack.

Then say the assumptions out loud and write them on the board: "I'll assume 10k daily users, English only, docs updated daily, human escalation allowed."

**Why it matters:** Interviewers grade structured thinking. Stated assumptions let you defend choices and let the interviewer correct you early instead of late.

**Failure modes:** asking 20 questions with no commitment, or silently assuming and building the wrong thing.

System design: turn ambiguity into assumptions (users, traffic, latency, quality, cost, freshness, privacy, reliability). Simplest architecture first. Whiteboard the stack: routing, RAG, tools, caches, DBs, inference, observability, evals, security, deploy. Enterprise: no public API, defend managed or self-host. Explain trade-offs, not logos. Practise support assistant, coding assistant, research agent, document intelligence. Timebox: requirements, one design, costs and eval. Cut the second agent, the graph, the extra reranker under pressure.

## What it is

**What it is:** Choosing which model serves which request, trading quality, latency, cost, context length, privacy and tool-use ability.

**How it works:** Use tiers: a small, cheap model for classification, extraction and easy chat; a frontier model for hard reasoning; a specialised or fine-tuned model where it earns its keep. A **router** picks per request, via rules (intent, length), a cheap classifier, or **cascading** (try small, escalate if confidence or a verifier is low). Add fallbacks across providers for outages.

**Example (illustrative):** 70% of tickets are simple; routing them to a small model could cut cost several-fold with a measured quality loss under 1 point on your eval set.

**Why it matters:** Model cost dominates LLM bills; routing is the biggest lever after caching.

**Failure modes:** router errors send hard queries to weak models; switching models silently changes behaviour, so re-run evals on every change; check current docs for model limits.

## What it is

**What it is:** Retrieval-augmented generation supplies relevant external text to the model at request time, and context management decides what fits in the prompt.

**How it works:** Ingest -> chunk -> embed -> index. At query time: rewrite query, hybrid search (keyword + vector), rerank, take top-k, assemble the prompt with citations. Context budget: system prompt + history + retrieved chunks + room for output; trim or summarise history.

**Design points to mention:** chunking by structure, metadata filters (tenant, ACL, date), freshness via re-indexing, citation and "I don't know" behaviour, and eval of retrieval (recall@k) separate from generation (faithfulness).

**Why it matters:** RAG is the default for grounding on private or changing data; cheaper and easier to update than fine-tuning.

**Failure modes:** poor chunks, missing ACL filters leaking data, too much context diluting attention, stale index, prompt injection inside retrieved text.

System design: turn ambiguity into assumptions (users, traffic, latency, quality, cost, freshness, privacy, reliability). Simplest architecture first. Whiteboard the stack: routing, RAG, tools, caches, DBs, inference, observability, evals, security, deploy. Enterprise: no public API, defend managed or self-host. Explain trade-offs, not logos. Practise support assistant, coding assistant, research agent, document intelligence. Timebox: requirements, one design, costs and eval. Cut the second agent, the graph, the extra reranker under pressure.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: RAG & context. RAG and context

On the job, rAG & context is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Forty-five minutes is enough for one design if you do not collect logos.

The concrete requirement is: RAG and context If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, requirements first, then one design, then cost and eval — and what you cut. A strong answer names this item (RAG & context) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

Treat “RAG & context” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. RAG and context

Support assistant: FAQ RAG + workflow, not an autonomous agent. You cut the graph DB and the second reranker when time is low.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “RAG & context” because the happy path works.** RAG and context Jumping to multi-agent before users and SLOs.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Naming six vendors and no eval.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement rag & context. No cut when they say “we have a week.”

## What you would say in 30 seconds

RAG & context: RAG and context Assumptions, simplest design, full stack in boxes, trade-offs not logos, cut under pressure, always eval and cost. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

You are on the hook for m15-6. A reviewer asks you to prove “RAG & context.” You timebox a coding assistant: repo RAG, tools with HITL on merge, cache, traces, eval on real PRs. You cut the research agent they baited.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements RAG and context You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

questions.q: Name the stages of a RAG pipeline and one failure at each.
questions.a: Ingest/chunk (bad splits lose meaning), embed/index (stale data), retrieve (misses relevant chunk), rerank, assemble prompt (overflow or dilution), generate (ignores context or hallucinates). Fix each with targeted evals.

questions.q: Users report answers citing documents they should not see. Cause and fix?
questions.a: Retrieval ignored access control. Store ACL metadata with each chunk and filter by the user's permissions in the query itself, not after generation; add a test with two users of different rights.

## What it is

**What it is:** Tools let a model call functions (search, SQL, ticket APIs); an agent loops: decide, call tool, observe, repeat until done.

**How it works:** Define tools with JSON schemas; the model emits a call; your code validates arguments, executes with least privilege, and returns results. Prefer a fixed workflow (prompt chain) when steps are known; use an agent only when the path is open-ended.

**Design points:** step and cost limits, timeouts, idempotency for writes, human approval for risky actions, tool results treated as untrusted, and traces of every step.

**Why it matters:** Agents add capability and unpredictability together: more latency, cost and failure modes.

**Failure modes:** infinite loops, wrong tool arguments, injected instructions in tool output, and destructive actions without confirmation. In interviews, justify "agent" against a simple workflow.

caches.explain:
## What it is

**What it is:** Layers that avoid recomputing expensive work.

**Types:**
- **Exact response cache:** key on normalised prompt + model + params; safe for deterministic, non-personal queries.
- **Semantic cache:** return a prior answer if the query embedding is within a threshold; risk of wrong hits.
- **Prompt (prefix) caching:** provider reuses the processed static prefix (system prompt, documents), cutting latency and input cost; keep stable content first.
- **Retrieval and embedding caches:** reuse embeddings and search results.
- **KV cache** inside inference servers.

**Why it matters:** Caching is the cheapest cost and latency win.

**Failure modes:** serving one user's answer to another (include tenant/permission in the key), stale answers after data change (TTL, invalidate on re-index), semantic threshold too loose, and caching unvalidated outputs. State what you would never cache: personalised or sensitive responses.

questions.q: Compare exact, semantic and prompt caching.
questions.a: Exact: identical request, safest. Semantic: similar queries by embedding, higher hit rate but risk of wrong answers. Prompt caching: reuses the processed prefix for latency and input cost, not the answer. Each has different keys and risks.

databases.explain:
## What it is

**What it is:** Choosing storage for each kind of AI data.

**Mapping:**
- **Relational (Postgres):** users, tickets, conversations, evals, config; transactions and joins. pgvector may suffice for modest vector needs.
- **Vector store / search engine:** embeddings plus metadata filters, hybrid keyword search.
- **Document/object store:** raw files, parsed text, artifacts.
- **Key-value/Redis:** sessions, rate limits, caches.
- **Queue:** async ingestion, batch jobs.
- **Warehouse:** analytics, eval history, logs.

**Trade-offs:** fewer systems means less operations; one Postgres with pgvector is often the right first answer. Separate stores when scale, filtering or latency demand it.

**Failure modes:** index and source of truth drifting apart, missing multi-tenant isolation, unbounded conversation logs holding personal data without retention rules.

inference-services.explain:
## What it is

**What it is:** How models are served: hosted APIs versus self-hosted engines.

**Hosted API:** fastest start, no GPU ops, pay per token, rate limits, data-policy considerations. **Self-hosted** (vLLM-style engines on GPUs): control, privacy, predictable cost at high steady volume, but you handle scaling, batching, GPU utilisation and upgrades.

**Key concepts:** streaming, continuous batching, KV cache, quantisation, autoscaling on queue depth, timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, provider fallback, and separate paths for interactive versus batch traffic.

**Why it matters:** Self-hosting only pays off at sufficient utilisation; idle GPUs are expensive.

**Failure modes:** retry storms during outages, no backpressure, cold starts, mixed batch and interactive load starving users. Mention rate-limit handling and budgets per tenant.

observability.explain:
## What it is

**What it is:** Seeing what the system did and why, per request.

**What to capture:** a **trace** per request with spans for retrieval, each LLM call, and each tool call; prompt version, model, parameters, token counts, latency (time to first token and total), cost, cache hit, retrieved IDs, guardrail results, user feedback. Redact personal data.

**Metrics and alerts:** p50/p95 latency, error rate, cost per request and per tenant, refusal rate, thumbs-down rate, retrieval empty-rate, quality scores from sampled online evals.

**Why it matters:** LLM failures are silent (plausible wrong text). Without traces you cannot debug, and without feedback loops you cannot improve; production traces feed the eval set.

**Failure modes:** logging raw sensitive prompts, too little context to reproduce, and dashboards with only infrastructure metrics.

System design: turn ambiguity into assumptions (users, traffic, latency, quality, cost, freshness, privacy, reliability). Simplest architecture first. ## What it is

**What it is:** Protecting data, actions and the model from misuse.

**Threats and controls:**

## What it is

**What it is:** A repeatable routine for deciding whether a new model, library or technique deserves your time.

**A simple process:**
1. **Triage (10 minutes):** what problem does it claim to solve, and do we have that problem?
2. **Map to your system:** which component would it replace or improve (cost, quality, latency, capability)?
3. **Small experiment:** run it on your own eval set or a few real cases.
4. **Decide:** adopt, watch, or ignore, and write down why.
5. **Timebox** exploration so it does not eat sprint time.

**Why it matters:** The field moves weekly; without a filter you either chase everything or fall behind. A process also gives you a strong interview answer.

**Failure modes:** evaluating on demos instead of your data, adopting for novelty, and never revisiting a "watch" decision. Keep a lightweight log of decisions.

how-would-you-halve-the-cost.explain:
## What it is

**What it is:** A cost-optimisation probe.

**Levers in order of effort:** (1) **Measure** cost per request by component; find the biggest part. (2) **Prompt caching** and response caching. (3) **Trim context:** fewer retrieved chunks, shorter history, compact instructions. (4) **Route** easy queries to smaller models. (5) **Batch** non-urgent work at discounted batch pricing (check current terms). (6) Limit output length. (7) Distil or fine-tune a small model for high-volume tasks. ## What it is

**What it is:** When you lack knowledge or data, propose how to find out instead of inventing facts.

## What it is

A **close** is **questions that show you understand their stack**, not generic culture prompts. Read their engineering blog. Ask about pins, gates, or how they deploy — something they actually run.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a close is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Performance is a separate skill from knowledge. Untimed answers lie.

The concrete requirement is: A **close** is **questions that show you understand their stack**, not generic culture prompts. Read their engineering blog. Ask about pins, gates, or how they deploy — something t If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, the loop itself — timed, recorded, scored — and a close that proves you heard their stack. A strong answer names this item (a close) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Write three questions from their posts. Example: “You mentioned CodeDeploy — how do you pin models behind the ALB?” not “What’s the culture?”

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “a close” because the happy path works.** A **close** is **questions that show you understand their stack**, not generic culture prompts. Read their engineering blog. Ask about pins, gates, or how they deploy — something t Untimed practice only.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Bluffing a paper you did not read.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement a close. Closing with “what is the culture?”

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I close on their stack, not on generic culture.

## A concrete walk-through

You ask one stack question and stop. That is the close.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need a close?” They ask a question you do not know. You say how you would measure it. You do not invent a vendor. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: A **close** is **questions that show you understand their stack**, not generic culture prompts. Read their engineering blog. Ask about pins, gates, or how they deploy — something t Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Mock count, scores by dimension, whether your close questions mention their actual systems. Also: time since you last exercised “a close” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “a close” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

Read their engineering blog. Ask about pins, gates, or how they deploy. “What’s the culture?” is a wasted close. Three stack questions written down is enough; ask one and stop.

## Practise until it is boring

Rehearse a close until you can name the artefact, the metric, and the undo without notes. If you cannot drill it, assume the control is dead. Write the last date you exercised it next to the cheat-sheet line.
